chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Mu'amar ibn Khallad, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:

I went out intending to visit Dawud ibn Isa ibn Ali, who was staying at Bi'r Maymoun. I was wearing two coarse garments. I saw an old woman with two young slave girls, so I said, 'O old woman, are these two girls being sold?' She said, 'Yes, but the likes of you cannot buy them.' I said, 'Why?' She said, 'Because one of them is a singer and the other is a musician.'

So I entered upon Dawud ibn Isa, and he raised me up and seated me in his place. When I left his presence, he said to his companions, 'Do you know who this is? This is Ali ibn Musa, whom the people of Iraq claim has obligatory obedience (due to him).'

key_terms.بِئْرَ مَيْمُونٍ: Bi'r Maymoun, a location in Kufa where Dawud ibn Isa resided
key_terms.مَفْرُوضُ الطَّاعَةِ: Obligatory obedience (referring to the Imam's authority)

ai.seo_question: What happened when Imam al-Rida visited Dawud ibn Isa?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Imam's humility and the recognition of his status by the Iraqi scholars, specifically Dawud ibn Isa, who acknowledges him as the one to whom obedience is obligatory (*Mafrud al-Ta'ah*). The narrative underscores the Shia doctrine of the Imam's divine authority and social visibility, contrasting his modest appearance with his elevated spiritual rank.
